quote: zum Ausrechnen bestimmter Aufgaben beruhen und wie man diese Vortheile rechnerisch abschätzen kann.
english: ...[on what the advantages of known arithmetic formulas and theorems] for computing specific problems rest, and how one can estimate these advantages computationally.
topic: Hilbert asks how the advantages of known arithmetic formulas (summation of arithmetic series, congruence formulas, Stirling's formula) for computing specific problems can be quantified by counting elementary operations, giving the digits of π and the computation of n! as examples.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert is asking for a measure of computational cost: a way to say exactly how much faster a closed formula or theorem (the arithmetic-series sum n(n+1)/2, congruence rules, Stirling's approximation of n!) makes a specific computation, compared with doing it directly. The cost would be the number of elementary operations needed, as a function of the input size. Examples would be how many operations it takes to get the first n digits of π, or to compute n!. In modern terms this is the program of computational complexity, and in particular algebraic (arithmetic) complexity: count the operations an algorithm needs (upper bounds) and the minimum any algorithm must need (lower bounds), then compare.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's question is a general program, not a single problem, so nobody 'answered' it in one step. The framework it asks for was built later by several people. Ostrowski (1954) proved that Horner's rule uses the minimum number of additions for evaluating a polynomial, an early lower bound of this kind. Hartmanis and Stearns, 'On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms' (1965), gave the general definitions of time and space complexity and won the 1993 Turing Award for it. Schönhage and Strassen (1970/71) showed how to multiply large integers quickly. Salamin and Brent (1975–76) found AGM-based methods for computing π, with Brent's paper titled 'Fast multiple-precision evaluation of elementary functions' (J. ACM 1976). Many specific questions inside the field are still open.

evidence.claim: Ostrowski proved in 1954 that Horner's rule uses the minimum number of additions for polynomial evaluation, an early example of exact operation counting with optimality proofs.
In algebraic complexity theory's arithmetic model, each base-field operation is counted at unit cost. This is the operation-counting measure Hilbert proposed.
Hartmanis and Stearns's 1965 paper 'On the Computational Complexity of Algorithms' defined quantified time and space complexity.
Hartmanis and Stearns received the 1993 Turing Award for the paper that founded computational complexity theory.
In 1970 Schönhage and Strassen gave a method to multiply n-digit integers with far fewer operations than the schoolbook method's O(n^2).
Salamin and Brent independently found AGM-based fast algorithms for π in 1975. Brent's 1976 J. ACM paper treats evaluating π and elementary functions as a question of computational complexity.
Operation-count complexities of standard arithmetic tasks (multiplication, and constants and functions such as π and the factorial) are now catalogued as standard knowledge.

triage.why: The note does not pose a precise theorem to prove. It asks how to put a number on the speed-up a formula gives by counting elementary operations, and that is the basic idea of algorithm analysis and algebraic complexity theory. The two examples, digits of π and n!, became standard topics in that field (AGM and fast-multiplication methods for π; fast algorithms for factorials). So the framework Hilbert asked for exists and is well established, which is why I chose 'solved'. Three caveats: (1) The answer came from many people over decades, not from one direct response to Hilbert. I found no source linking this note to that later work, and I could not find the page or confirm its date. (2) The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 published problems or the 24th problem. (3) Many specific lower-bound questions in arithmetic complexity are still actively researched. I didn't manage to find a source for the exact current best results on computing n!, because my search limit ran out.
